reference.source: Oral medicine and dermatology reference texts
clinicalPearls: A chronic immune-mediated mucosal disorder presenting with bilateral, often symmetrical, white striae, plaques, atrophic or erosive lesions
The reticular form with lacy white Wickham striae is frequently asymptomatic, whereas erosive and atrophic forms cause pain and burning
The buccal mucosa, tongue and gingivae are commonly involved, and desquamative gingivitis may be the presenting feature
A lichenoid reaction that is clinically similar can be caused by drugs, dental materials or graft-versus-host disease
There is a small but recognised risk of malignant transformation, so long-term monitoring is advised
Topical corticosteroids are the mainstay for symptomatic disease, with other immunomodulators for refractory cases
reference.pathophysiology: Oral lichen planus is a T-cell-mediated chronic inflammatory condition in which cytotoxic T lymphocytes target basal keratinocytes of the mucosal epithelium, producing basal cell damage and a band-like subepithelial lymphocytic infiltrate. The resulting epithelial changes create the characteristic striae, atrophy and erosions. Similar lichenoid reactions can be triggered by drugs, contact with dental restorative materials or systemic graft-versus-host disease, reflecting a shared final immunological pathway.
additionalDifferentials: Oral lichenoid drug or contact reaction
additionalInvestigations: Clinical assessment of distribution and morphology
Biopsy with histopathology, and direct immunofluorescence to exclude immunobullous disease
Review of medications and dental materials for lichenoid triggers
Long-term surveillance for malignant change, especially in erosive disease
Assessment for cutaneous or other mucosal lichen planus
redFlags: Non-homogeneous, indurated or non-healing areas suggesting dysplasia or carcinoma
Features suggesting immunobullous disease requiring different management
reference.prognosis: The condition is chronic with relapses and remissions; symptoms are usually controllable, but erosive forms carry a small long-term risk of malignant transformation requiring surveillance.
pitfalls: Not distinguishing lichen planus from a lichenoid drug or contact reaction
Missing an immunobullous disorder presenting as desquamative gingivitis
Failing to monitor for malignant transformation
Overlooking coexisting skin or genital lichen planus
management: Use topical corticosteroids as first-line therapy for symptomatic erosive or atrophic disease
Add topical calcineurin inhibitors (tacrolimus) for lesions refractory to topical steroids
Reserve systemic corticosteroids or steroid-sparing immunomodulators for severe or widespread refractory disease
Provide symptomatic measures: analgesic or anaesthetic mouthwashes, meticulous oral hygiene, avoidance of spicy and acidic foods, and treatment of superimposed candidiasis
Identify and remove lichenoid triggers such as culprit drugs and adjacent dental restorative materials
Maintain long-term surveillance for malignant transformation, particularly in erosive disease
Refer to oral medicine or dermatology and assess for cutaneous and other mucosal lichen planus
